items.title: Sonny Rollins — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: He was my clarinet teacher, as a matter of fact.

ctx.x: Could you recognize where somebody is from in the city from the way they play?

Uh...no. I never got to that point where I could do that, you know. No. And the guys in the Bronx–of course, Monk was in the Bronx...uh lived in the Bronx for a while, and Elmo Hope, my piano player...well, a piano player that I was associated with, he lived in the Bronx–and uh...a very fine um reedman, Eddie Barefield, he lived in the Bronx. He was my clarinet teacher, as a matter of fact. He was a splendid person. Uh, Eddie lived in the Bronx. So, I don’t think there was any discernible stylistic differences,
you know, that you could say, “Oh, that’s a Bronx sound,” or something. I, I don’t think I would say that.

items.title: 52060_Eddie Barefield oral history interview
items.q: And he studied with me for a while. But he and Max Roach both studied writing with me.

ctx.x: But, see, I went more for the Benny Carter type of playing because Benny had the -- I always like the sound, I like a certain sound. Although, right now I still -- I listen to Don Byas and I hear a lot of Bird's passages now that Don plays. But he had the sound that was such a warm musical sound that it makes it -- I have a lot of records by Coltrane and I listen to Coltrane. He sounded like a beginner when you listen to Don Byas afterwards, although he was great. Great saxophone player but none of them go for…
Well, would you say Sonny Rollins has more of a sound?

Well, Sonny is unpredictible. He plays all kinds of things. He can play with sound, he plays some things that I wonder if he's going crazy, or what. And he studied with me for a while. But he and Max Roach both studied writing with me. And Sonny wanted to learn the clarinet but he gave it up.
